items.prompt: Which command runs a JavaScript file named `app.js` with Node.js?

options.label: `js run app.js`
`node app.js`
`nodejs install app.js`
`npm app.js`

rubric: `node` followed by the file name runs the file in the runtime.
`npm` manages packages and does not run files directly.

items.prompt: Which file lists a Node.js project's name, scripts and dependencies?

options.label: `package.json`
`index.config`
`dependencies.js`
`node_modules.json`

rubric: `package.json` is the project manifest created by `npm init`.
The other names do not exist as standard npm files.

items.prompt: In CommonJS, which call loads the built-in `fs` module?

options.label: `include('fs')`
`using('fs')`
`require('fs')`
`load.module('fs')`

rubric: `require` is the CommonJS function for importing modules.
The others are not Node.js functions.

items.prompt: Which built-in Node.js module is used to read and write files?

options.label: `url`
`os`
`fs`
`path`

rubric: `fs` is the file system module.
`path` only manipulates path strings, `os` reports system info, `url` parses URLs.

items.prompt: Which command installs the `express` package into a project?

options.label: `npm install express`
`npm fetch express`
`npm run express`
`node install express`

rubric: `npm install <name>` downloads a package and adds it to dependencies.
`node` and `npm run` do not install packages.

items.prompt: Which of these are built-in Node.js core modules that need no npm install? Select all that apply.

options.label: `path`
`express`
`http`
`fs`
`lodash`

rubric: `http`, `path` and `fs` ship with Node.js.
`express` and `lodash` are third-party npm packages.

items.prompt: Maria has created an Express app object named `app` and defined a route. She now wants the server to start accepting requests on port 3000. Which call does she make?

options.label: `app.open(3000)`
`app.serve(3000)`
`app.listen(3000)`
`app.start(3000)`

rubric: `app.listen(port)` starts the HTTP server on that port.
The other method names do not exist in Express.

items.prompt: What does this print? `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); console.log('C');`

options.label: `C A B`
`A C B`
`A B C`
`B A C`

rubric: The timer callback runs only after the current synchronous code finishes.
A 0 ms delay does not mean immediate execution.

items.prompt: Why can Node.js handle many requests with a single JavaScript thread?

options.label: It starts a new JavaScript thread for each request and closes it after replying
It hands I/O work off and runs callbacks via the event loop when done
It pauses each request until the previous one has fully finished
It compiles the code to run in parallel on every CPU core

rubric: The event loop lets I/O run in the background and queues callbacks.
Node does not create one JS thread per request.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of `devDependencies` in `package.json`?

options.label: Packages that the production server must always install
Packages that are loaded before every other dependency
Packages needed only during development, such as test tools
Packages that run only on the developer's own operating system

rubric: devDependencies hold tools needed for building and testing.
They are not required for the app to run in production.

items.prompt: What does assigning a value to `module.exports` in a file do?

options.label: It writes the value to a file on disk so later runs can reload it
It makes the value available to files that `require` it
It runs the file again each time it changes, like a file watcher
It marks the value as private so that no other file can access it

rubric: `module.exports` defines what `require` returns for that file.
It does not persist or hide anything.

items.prompt: Why is `fs.readFileSync` described as a blocking call?

options.label: It reads the file in a separate thread while code continues
It can only read files that are small enough for memory
It stops other JavaScript running until the read completes
It locks the file so no other program can open it

rubric: Sync methods halt the event loop until the work is finished.
Blocking refers to JavaScript execution, not file locks.

items.prompt: Which statements about npm are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It compiles JavaScript files into machine code
It replaces the Node.js runtime when running code
It records installed packages in `package.json`
It downloads packages into a `node_modules` folder
It can run scripts defined under `scripts` in `package.json`

rubric: npm installs packages, records them and runs scripts.
It is a package manager, not a compiler or a runtime.

items.prompt: A developer's Express server reads a large file with `fs.readFileSync` inside a route handler. While one user requests that route, other users' requests to simple routes are delayed. What explains this?

options.label: Express limits each server process to handling one connected user at a time
The synchronous read blocks the single thread, so other requests wait
Node.js queues requests by route name and always serves the largest file routes first
The file read uses up all the available network bandwidth for other users

rubric: Sync I/O blocks the event loop, so no other callbacks run.
Delay comes from the blocked thread, not bandwidth or Express limits.

items.prompt: In a CommonJS file, what does the line `module.exports = { add }` do?

options.label: It adds `add` to the global object so every file in the project can call it
It publishes `add` to the npm registry for other developers
It runs `add` once as soon as the file is loaded
It lets other files get `add` by calling `require` on this file

rubric: `module.exports` defines what `require` returns for this file.
Distractors confuse module exports with globals, execution on load, or npm publishing.

items.prompt: Why can a single Node.js process serve many network connections without a thread per connection?

options.label: Slow I/O is handed off and its callback is queued to run on the event loop when ready
Each connection is automatically copied into its own operating system process
Node compiles JavaScript into parallel machine code that runs on every CPU core
Node pauses each connection until the previous one has finished its response

rubric: I/O is non-blocking; completed work queues callbacks on the event loop.
Distractors suggest automatic multiprocessing or sequential handling.

items.prompt: A project uses the test runner `jest` only while developing. In `package.json`, where does it belong?

options.label: `devDependencies`, because it is needed only for development and testing
`scripts`, because tests are run by a script
`main`, because it is the entry point for tests
`dependencies`, because every package must be listed there to install

rubric: Tools used only in development go in devDependencies.
Distractors confuse scripts or main with dependency categories.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the `package-lock.json` file?

options.label: It lists the scripts that `npm run` is allowed to execute in the project
It records the exact versions installed so installs are reproducible
It locks `package.json` so other developers cannot edit the dependency list
It encrypts the packages stored in `node_modules` so they cannot be tampered with

rubric: The lock file pins exact resolved versions of the dependency tree.
Distractors treat it as a security, permission or script file.

items.prompt: When you run `node tool.js build`, what does `process.argv` contain?

options.label: Only the string `build`
An array: the node path, the script path, then `build`
An object with the keys `node`, `tool.js` and `build`
The environment variables that were set for the process

rubric: argv is an array whose first two entries are the node executable and script path.
Distractors think only user arguments are included or confuse it with env.

items.prompt: Which statements about Node's `fs` module are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: `fs.promises.readFile` returns a promise that resolves with the file contents
`fs.readFile` runs its callback before the next line of code executes
`fs.readFile` callbacks receive the data first and the error second
`fs.readFileSync` blocks the event loop until the file has been read

rubric: Sync calls block; the promises API returns promises.
Callbacks are error-first and run later, not immediately.

items.prompt: A developer's web server calls `fs.readFileSync` on a 500 MB log file inside a request handler. While one user requests it, other users' simple requests all stall. What best explains this?

options.label: Express pauses its router while any file is open, so queued requests wait until the file handle is closed
The synchronous read blocks the single JavaScript thread, so the event loop cannot serve other requests
Node allows only one open file descriptor per process, so other requests wait until that file is released
The 500 MB file is cached in memory, which fills the network buffer and leaves no room for other users' responses

rubric: Sync I/O blocks the event loop thread that serves all requests.
Distractors invent file-handle, caching or Express limits.

items.prompt:
What does this script print, in order?
`console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`

options.label: A D B C
A B C D
A C D B
A D C B

rubric: Sync logs run first, then the promise microtask, then the timer callback.
Distractors treat setTimeout 0 as immediate or run promises before sync code.

items.prompt: An Express app defines `app.get('/users/:id', handler)`. A client requests `/users/42`. What is `req.params.id` inside the handler?

options.label: The string `'42'`
`undefined`, because ids must be in `req.query`
The string `'/users/42'`
The number `42`

rubric: Route parameters are always strings.
Distractors confuse params with query, or expect numeric conversion.

items.prompt: You want to add `eslint` as a tool used only during development. Which command does that?

options.label: `npm run eslint --save`
`npm install --save-dev eslint`
`npm init eslint --dev`
`npm install eslint --global-only`

rubric: `--save-dev` adds the package to devDependencies.
Distractors use invalid flags or the wrong npm subcommand.

items.prompt: A project's `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Which line correctly loads the file system module in a `.js` file?

options.label: `include fs from 'node:fs'`
`import fs from 'node:fs'`
`import fs = require('fs')`
`const fs = require('fs')`

rubric: With type module, .js files use ES module import syntax.
Distractors use CommonJS, a nonexistent keyword, or TypeScript-only syntax.

items.prompt: A POST route in Express logs `req.body` as `undefined` when the client sends JSON. Which change fixes it?

options.label: Call `app.use(express.json())` before the route definitions
Add `app.use(express.json())` after the last route definition
Rename the route handler to use `req.json` instead
Convert the route to `app.get` so the body is parsed

rubric: Body-parsing middleware must be registered before the routes that need it.
Distractors misplace the middleware or change the HTTP method.

items.prompt: A script is started with `node app.js hello`. Which expressions evaluate to the string `'hello'`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `process.argv.slice(2)[0]`
`process.argv[1]`
`process.argv[0]`
`process.argv[2]`

rubric: Index 2 is the first user argument; slice(2) drops node and script paths.
Indexes 0 and 1 hold the node path and script path.

items.prompt: A developer writes an Express route: `app.get('/log', (req, res) => { let text; fs.readFile('app.log', 'utf8', (err, data) => { text = data; }); res.send(text); });` Requests always return an empty response. Which fix works?

options.label: Declare `text` with `const` so it is set before sending
Move `res.send(data)` inside the callback, after handling `err`
Use `fs.readFile` with the `'utf8'` argument removed
Replace `res.send` with `res.end` after the `readFile` call

rubric: The callback runs later, so the response must be sent inside it.
Distractors keep the send outside the async callback.

items.prompt:
What does this script print, in order?

`console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); process.nextTick(() => console.log('C')); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('D')); console.log('E');`

options.label: A E D C B
A E C D B
A E B C D
A C D E B

rubric: Synchronous logs run first, then the nextTick queue, then promise microtasks, then the timer callback.
Distractors swap nextTick and promise order or treat the 0ms timer as immediate.

items.prompt: In an ES module, which line correctly loads and parses `config.json` with `import fs from 'node:fs/promises'`?

options.label: `const cfg = await JSON.parse('config.json')`
`const cfg = JSON.parse(await fs.readFileSync('config.json', 'utf8'))`
`const cfg = JSON.parse(fs.readFile('config.json', 'utf8'))`
`const cfg = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('config.json', 'utf8'))`

rubric: The promise from readFile must be awaited before parsing the string.
Distractors pass a pending promise to JSON.parse, parse a filename, or mix sync with a callback.

items.prompt: An Express 4 app has several routes. Where must you register a centralised error handler so it catches errors passed with `next(err)` from those routes?

options.label: After all routes, as `app.use((err, req, res, next) => ...)`
Before all routes, as `app.use((err, req, res, next) => ...)`
After all routes, as `app.use((req, res) => ...)`
Before all routes, as `app.use((req, res, next) => ...)`

rubric: Error middleware needs four parameters and must be registered after the routes.
Distractors get the arity or the registration order wrong.

items.prompt: You run `node tool.js --name Ada`. What is the value of `process.argv[2]` inside `tool.js`?

options.label: `'--name'`
`'node'`
`'tool.js'`
`'Ada'`

rubric: argv[0] is the node binary, argv[1] is the script path, and user arguments start at index 2.
Distractors assume flags are parsed or that indexing starts at the script.

items.prompt: A CommonJS file contains `exports.a = 1; module.exports = { b: 2 };`. What does `require` return for this file?
rubric: require returns module.exports, which was reassigned to a new object, so the earlier exports.a is lost.
Distractors assume the objects are merged or that the exports alias wins.

items.prompt: You must send a 2 GB file in an HTTP response without loading it all into memory. Which approaches do this correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: `await pipeline(fs.createReadStream(path), res)` using `stream/promises`
`res.end(await fs.promises.readFile(path))`
`res.end(fs.readFileSync(path))`
`fs.createReadStream(path).pipe(res)`

rubric: Both stream the file in chunks with backpressure handling.
The readFile variants buffer the whole file in memory first; the async one is not safer.

items.prompt: Your team deploys a Node service from CI. `package.json` lists `"express": "^4.18.0"` and a committed `package-lock.json` pins 4.18.2. Builds must install exactly the locked versions and fail if the lock file and package.json disagree. Which command should the CI script run?

options.label: `npm install express@latest`
`npm update`
`npm install --no-save`
`npm ci`

rubric: npm ci installs exactly from the lock file and errors if it is out of sync with package.json.
npm install and update may change resolved versions within the caret range.

items.prompt: An Express 4 route is `app.get('/u', async (req, res) => { const u = await db.find(); res.json(u); })`. When `db.find()` rejects, the client request hangs. What is the underlying cause?

options.label: Express 4 ignores the promise the handler returns, so the rejection never reaches error middleware
Calling `res.json` after an `await` detaches the response from the request, so the reply is never flushed
Express 4 runs async handlers on a separate worker thread, and that thread times out on rejection
Express 4 catches the rejection, but its default error handler skips routes declared as async functions

rubric: Express 4 ignores the returned promise, so a rejection is unhandled and no response is sent.
Distractors invent restrictions on await, threads or the default handler.

items.prompt: A script reads 500 small files with `for (const f of files) { results.push(await fs.readFile(f, 'utf8')); }` and takes far longer than expected. Which diagnosis best explains it?

options.label: The loop creates 500 promises at once, which overloads the thread pool
`await` inside a loop blocks the whole event loop until each file finishes
`fs.readFile` always runs on the main thread, so reads cannot overlap
Each read starts only after the previous one finishes, so no I/O overlaps

rubric: Sequential awaits serialise the reads; starting them together and using Promise.all would overlap them.
await does not block the event loop, and the loop does not start reads concurrently.

items.prompt: A Node HTTP server's `/report` handler runs a 3-second synchronous loop to build a summary. During that time `/health` requests time out. What is the cause?

options.label: The synchronous loop occupies the single JS thread, so no other callbacks run
The report handler uses up all of libuv's worker threads, so /health has none left
Node accepts only one open connection at a time, so /health waits for /report to end
`/health` is queued behind `/report` by the HTTP keep-alive setting on the socket

rubric: CPU-bound sync code blocks the event loop, stalling every other request.
Distractors blame the thread pool, connection limits, or keep-alive instead of the blocked loop.

items.prompt: A process crashes with an uncaught exception even though the code is wrapped as `try { fs.readFile(p, (err, d) => { if (err) throw err; use(d); }); } catch (e) { log(e); }`. Which is the faulty step?

options.label: `readFile` rethrows most I/O errors straight to the process, bypassing the surrounding try/catch block
The `catch` block only receives errors whose type matches, so `ENOENT` errors are skipped here
The throw runs later in a callback, after the try block has already exited
`err` is usually null inside `readFile` callbacks, so the `if` check never takes effect

rubric: The callback runs on a later tick, outside the try/catch stack, so the throw is uncaught.
Distractors misread catch semantics or the callback's err argument.

items.prompt: After adding `"type": "module"` to `package.json`, `node app.js` fails with `ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope`. What is the cause?

options.label: The `express` package is not installed with ESM support
`.js` files are now treated as ES modules, where `require` is not provided
Node dropped support for the `require` function in all newer versions
`require` needs a `.cjs` extension on every call such as `require('x.cjs')`

rubric: The type field switches .js files to ESM, where require is not a global; use import or createRequire.
Distractors blame Node versions, call syntax or a specific package.

items.prompt: A long-running Express server's memory grows steadily with traffic. Which code patterns are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: A module-level `Map` gains an entry per request and nothing ever deletes entries
Each request adds a listener to a shared `EventEmitter` and never removes it
Handlers declare `const` variables for the request body
Large uploads are handled with `stream.pipeline` to disk

rubric: Unbounded caches and accumulating listeners retain objects for the process lifetime.
Request-scoped consts are collected after the request, and piping streams keeps memory flat.

items.prompt: A developer logs `setTimeout` and `setImmediate` callbacks, both scheduled from the main module. The order varies between runs. Scheduled inside an `fs.readFile` callback, `setImmediate` always fires first. Why is the order deterministic in the second case?

options.label: I/O callbacks run as microtasks, so they drain before any timer callback can run
The I/O callback runs in the poll phase, and the check phase comes before timers
`setImmediate` has higher priority than timers in every phase of the event loop
`fs.readFile` callbacks delay timers by at least one millisecond after they finish

rubric: After the poll phase the loop enters the check phase (setImmediate) before returning to timers.
From the main module the order depends on process timing; distractors invent priorities or microtask behaviour.

items.prompt: Inside an `fs.readFile` callback, code calls `setTimeout(() => log('T'), 0)`, `setImmediate(() => log('I'))`, `process.nextTick(() => log('N'))` and `Promise.resolve().then(() => log('P'))`, in that order. What is the logged order?

options.label: P, N, T, I
N, P, T, I
I, N, P, T
N, P, I, T

rubric: After an I/O callback the loop moves to the check phase before timers, so setImmediate beats setTimeout; nextTick runs before promise microtasks.
Distractors assume timers always fire first or that promises outrank nextTick.

items.prompt: An Express API normally answers in 20 ms. When one client posts a 60 MB JSON body, every other client sees multi-second latency until it finishes. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: The libuv thread pool is saturated by the upload socket, and sockets use that pool, so other connections must wait for it
Node opens one thread per request, and the large body exhausts the thread pool so other requests queue for a free thread
Express serialises all requests per route, so a slow request on a route blocks every other request that uses that route
`JSON.parse` of the body runs synchronously on the main thread, so the event loop cannot serve other requests meanwhile

rubric: Synchronous parsing of big payloads blocks the single JS thread and stalls all requests.
Distractors misattribute the stall to per-request threads, the libuv pool (sockets do not use it) or route-level queues.

items.prompt: A long-running service shows steadily growing memory and a `MaxListenersExceededWarning`. Each request handler runs `bus.on('update', onUpdate)` on a module-level EventEmitter and never removes it. What is the root cause?

options.label: The emitter copies every emitted event into a buffer per listener, and the buffers pile up because events are emitted too quickly
The warning shows the V8 heap limit was reached, and the listeners are only a symptom of the heap being too small for the load
Node caches the handler function for each route, so repeated registration creates duplicate cached entries that are never evicted
Each request adds a new listener that closes over request state; the shared emitter keeps them all reachable, so they are never collected

rubric: Listeners registered per request on a long-lived emitter keep their closures alive: a leak.
Distractors invent per-listener buffers, route caches or blame heap size.

items.prompt: After adding `"type": "module"` to package.json and renaming nothing else, a script fails with `ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined`. Why?

options.label: ES modules run in strict mode, which forbids reading globals that were defined implicitly, and `__dirname` is one such global
`__dirname` is injected by the CommonJS module wrapper, which ES modules do not use, so it must be derived from `import.meta.url`
The `type` field changes the working directory to the package root, so `__dirname` is no longer meaningful in any script
`__dirname` was removed from Node when ES modules became stable, so every project must now use `process.cwd()` for paths instead

rubric: The CJS wrapper provides __dirname; ESM instead exposes import.meta.url.
Distractors claim removal, strict-mode restrictions, or a changed working directory.

items.prompt: A script reads a 5 GB file with `createReadStream` and, in `on('data')`, calls `slowWriter.write(chunk)` while ignoring its return value. Memory climbs to several GB. What explains this?

options.label: The read stream loads the whole file into memory first, then emits chunks from that copy, so memory matches the file size
`write()` returns false when its buffer is full, but ignoring it keeps queueing chunks because the reader is never paused
Chunks are copied twice by `on('data')`, which doubles memory use for any file larger than the default highWaterMark of the stream
The garbage collector cannot free Buffers that came from a file stream, so memory grows with every chunk whatever the writer does

rubric: Without honouring backpressure (pause until 'drain', or use pipeline) the writable buffer grows unbounded.
Distractors misunderstand streaming, chunk copying or Buffer collection.

items.prompt: Which of these in an HTTP request handler would block the event loop and hurt other clients' latency? Select all that apply.

options.label: `fs.readFileSync('big.json')` on every request
`await fetch(url)` to a slow upstream service
`await fs.promises.readFile('big.json')`
`crypto.pbkdf2Sync` with a high iteration count to hash a password
A `for` loop summing 500 million numbers before responding

rubric: Sync file I/O, sync crypto and long CPU loops all occupy the main thread.
Awaiting async I/O yields to the loop, so waiting on fs.promises or fetch does not block.

items.prompt: A team runs an Express app with the `cluster` module on 4 workers. Sessions are kept in a plain in-process object. Users report being randomly logged out, and it happens even though the server never restarts. Which analysis explains it?

options.label: Cookies are only valid for one worker's port, so the browser drops the session cookie when the balancer changes workers
The master process clears worker memory periodically to prevent leaks, which deletes the sessions after a short period
Cluster workers share one event loop, so concurrent requests overwrite each other's session objects in the shared object
Each worker has its own memory, so a session created in one worker is missing when the next request lands on another

rubric: Workers are separate processes with isolated memory; sessions need a shared store such as Redis.
Distractors invent memory clearing, a shared loop or per-worker cookie ports.

items.prompt: A Node API must resize user-uploaded images (about 300 ms CPU each) at up to 50 per second. Criteria: keep API latency low, reuse memory cheaply, avoid managing extra services. Which design is best?

options.label: A separate queue service and fleet of resizer machines, so the API process holds no image-processing code at all
A new `child_process.fork` per upload, so each image has a fully isolated process that exits after finishing
A `worker_threads` pool sized near the CPU core count, receiving buffers from the main thread and returning results
Resizing inline in the request handler with an async function, since `async` keeps the work off the main thread

rubric: A bounded thread pool keeps CPU work off the event loop with low overhead and no extra infrastructure.
Distractors: async does not move CPU work off-thread; forking per upload is costly; a separate fleet violates the no-extra-services criterion.

items.prompt: Express 4 handler: `app.get('/u/:id', async (req, res) => { const u = await db.find(req.params.id); res.json(u); })`. Criteria: failed lookups must return a 500 via the error middleware, with no process crash and little repetition across 40 routes. Which approach is best?

options.label: Put a `try/catch` around `app.listen` so errors thrown inside any handler are caught at startup
Add `process.on('unhandledRejection', () => {})` so rejections are swallowed and the process stays up
Wrap async handlers in a small helper that catches rejections and calls `next(err)`, applied to every route
Rewrite each handler with a nested callback style, because Express 4 only supports callbacks for database errors

rubric: Express 4 does not forward rejected promises to error middleware; a wrapper does this once for all routes.
Distractors swallow errors globally, catch at the wrong scope, or misstate Express.

items.prompt: A server must send 2 GB video files to many concurrent clients. Criteria: bounded memory per request, correct handling of slow clients, minimal code. Which option is best?

options.label: Read the file in a loop with `readFile` on slices and call `res.write` on each, without checking its return value
`res.end(await fs.promises.readFile(path))`, since the promise API avoids blocking the event loop
`stream.pipeline(fs.createReadStream(path), res, cb)`, which applies backpressure and cleans up on errors
`res.end(fs.readFileSync(path))`, because a single synchronous read is the fastest way to get bytes out

rubric: pipeline streams chunks with backpressure and cleanup, keeping memory bounded.
Whole-file reads cost 2 GB per request; unchecked write loops ignore slow clients.

items.prompt: A CI pipeline must build the same dependency tree every run, fail if package.json and the lockfile disagree, and start from a clean node_modules. Which install command best meets these criteria?

options.label: `npm ci`
`npm install --no-save`
`npm update`
`npm install`

rubric: npm ci installs exactly from the lockfile, errors on mismatch and removes existing node_modules.
npm install and update may modify the lockfile or resolve newer versions.

items.prompt: A containerised HTTP service is redeployed often. Criteria: no dropped in-flight requests, no hung deploys, exit with the right status. Which SIGTERM handling is best?

options.label: Call `process.exit(0)` immediately in the handler so the container stops as fast as possible
Call `server.close()`, finish in-flight requests, then exit, with a timer that forces exit if draining takes too long
Call `server.close()` and leave the process running indefinitely, relying on the orchestrator to restart it after a while
Ignore SIGTERM and wait for the orchestrator to send SIGKILL, which stops the process cleanly after its grace period

rubric: Draining with a safety timeout satisfies all three criteria.
Immediate exit drops requests; ignoring SIGTERM or never exiting causes hung or forced kills.

items.prompt: A proposal stores all uploads with multer `memoryStorage()` for files up to 200 MB, on a 1 GB instance with about 30 concurrent uploads at peak. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Peak buffered data could reach about 6 GB, exceeding the instance's memory
Memory buffers stop the event loop from serving requests while an upload is in progress
`memoryStorage()` cannot access `req.file.buffer`, so the files cannot be processed
A few concurrent large uploads could crash the process with out-of-memory errors
Streaming to disk or object storage would keep per-request memory bounded

rubric: 30 x 200 MB far exceeds 1 GB; streaming avoids holding whole files in memory.
Buffering does not block the loop by itself, and the buffer property does exist.

items.prompt: An API runs on 6 identical instances behind a load balancer. You must cap each API key at 100 requests per minute across the fleet, with a low-latency check and no over-admission beyond a small margin. Which design best meets this?

options.label: An in-memory counter per instance, with the limit set to 100 so each instance enforces the full cap
A shared Redis store with atomic increments and key expiry, checked in middleware on each request
An in-memory counter per instance with the limit set to 17, assuming the balancer spreads traffic evenly
A counter in a JSON file on each instance, rewritten per request, so counts survive restarts

rubric: A shared atomic store enforces one global limit at low latency.
Per-instance counters admit up to 600 or rely on perfectly even balancing; file counters are slow and still per-instance.

items.prompt: An API handler hashes uploaded files with a CPU-heavy function (about 300 ms each). Criteria: other requests keep low p99 latency, no new infrastructure, and bounded CPU use. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Send hash jobs to a fixed-size `worker_threads` pool, keeping the main loop free and CPU use capped
Run the hash inline in the handler and rely on `await` to yield to other requests while it runs
Wrap the hash in `new Promise` so its execution is deferred and it no longer blocks the event loop
Spawn a new `worker_threads` Worker for every request, so each hash gets full isolation from the main loop

rubric: A fixed pool moves CPU work off the event loop and bounds concurrency.
Inline or Promise-wrapped work still runs on the main thread; one Worker per request has unbounded startup and memory cost.

items.prompt: A route must send multi-GB files to slow clients. Criteria: constant memory, correct handling of slow clients, and errors that destroy both streams and clean up. Which implementation is best?

options.label: `rs.on('data', c => res.write(c))`, which sends each chunk as soon as it is read from disk
`res.end(await fs.promises.readFile(p))`, which is simple and lets the runtime manage the buffer size
`rs.pipe(res)` alone, which handles backpressure and also destroys the source stream if the client disconnects mid-transfer
`stream.pipeline(fs.createReadStream(p), res, cb)`, which applies backpressure and destroys both streams on error

rubric: pipeline gives backpressure plus error and close propagation.
Plain pipe does not destroy the source on destination errors; ignoring write() return values buffers unboundedly.

items.prompt: A colleague claims: "Putting the 2-second synchronous loop inside an `async` function or a `new Promise` executor stops it blocking the server." Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The claim is false: both run their synchronous body on the main thread, so the loop still blocks until it ends
The claim holds, because anything inside a Promise is scheduled on the libuv thread pool
The claim is false because Promise callbacks run in a separate microtask thread that competes for the CPU
The claim holds only for `async` functions, since the `await` keyword always yields before the loop

rubric: Promise executors and async function bodies run synchronously until the first await, on the main thread.
Distractors assume Promises imply threads or thread pool offloading.

items.prompt: After an `uncaughtException`, which policy best meets these criteria: no corrupted state served to users, diagnosable failures, and fast recovery under a process supervisor?

options.label: Swallow the error in a handler and continue, because restarts drop in-flight work and hurt availability
Disable the handler so Node prints the trace, since logging inside it risks recursion and masked errors
Log with context, stop accepting new work, exit non-zero after a short timeout, and let the supervisor restart
Retry the failing operation inside the handler, since the stack is intact and state is therefore trustworthy

rubric: After an uncaught exception state is undefined; log and exit, then restart cleanly.
Continuing or retrying assumes state is intact; removing the handler loses structured logging and graceful draining.

items.prompt: A CI pipeline must give byte-for-byte reproducible dependency trees, fail if `package.json` and the lockfile disagree, and start from a clean `node_modules`. Which install step best meets the criteria?

options.label: `npm update && npm install`, since it ensures the newest patch versions are always tested and then saved
`npm install --no-save`, since it avoids modifying the lockfile and still fails when the manifest and lockfile disagree
`npm ci`, since it installs strictly from the lockfile, errors on mismatch and removes `node_modules`
`npm install`, since it reconciles the manifest with the lockfile automatically and keeps existing modules in place

rubric: npm ci is strict, lockfile-driven and clean.
npm install may rewrite the lockfile and tolerate drift; update changes versions.

items.prompt: A job must call a partner API 1,000 times, independently, and the partner allows at most 20 concurrent requests. Which approaches satisfy the limit while avoiding needless serial waiting? Select all that apply.

options.label: A pool such as `p-limit(20)` wrapping each call, awaited with `Promise.all`
Process the list in chunks of 20, awaiting `Promise.all` on each chunk before the next
`await Promise.all(urls.map(fetchOne))` with no further control
A `for` loop with `await` on each call, one at a time
`urls.forEach(async u => fetchOne(u))` so each call starts in the background

rubric: A pool and chunking both cap concurrency at 20 while running calls in parallel.
Promise.all over everything and forEach fire all 1,000; serial await is safe but wastes time.

items.prompt: Your Node HTTP service runs in containers behind a load balancer. During deploys, the orchestrator sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 30 seconds. Currently the handler calls `process.exit(0)` and users see dropped requests. Criteria: no in-flight request is lost, exit within the grace period, no hung shutdown. Which change is best?

options.label: Keep `process.exit(0)` but call it inside a 5-second `setTimeout` after SIGTERM, since most requests finish within that window
Call `server.close()` and exit only in its callback, since it waits for every open connection, so no timer is needed
Call `server.close()`, exit in its callback once requests drain, and add a forced-exit timer under 30 s
Ignore SIGTERM and let the orchestrator's SIGKILL end the process after 30 s, so the app never exits mid-request

rubric: Stop accepting, drain, then exit, with a fallback timer for stuck connections.
Fixed delay is arbitrary; ignoring SIGTERM kills abruptly; close() alone can hang on idle keep-alive connections.

items.prompt: Design a CLI that counts ERROR lines in a multi-GB log. Constraints: constant memory, correct with CRLF endings, and correct when a line spans two read chunks. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: `fs.readFileSync(f,'utf8').split('\n')`, then filter lines that include ERROR and trim the trailing `\r`
`createReadStream(f).on('data', c => c.toString().split(/\r?\n/))`, counting ERROR in each piece
`readline.createInterface({input: fs.createReadStream(f), crlfDelay: Infinity})` with `for await`
`fs.promises.readFile(f)` then split on `\r?\n`, since async reads avoid blocking the loop

rubric: readline buffers partial lines across chunks, handles CRLF and streams.
Whole-file reads break memory; per-chunk split misses lines spanning chunks.

items.prompt: Design the `package.json` of a library that must be consumable via both `require('lib')` and `import 'lib'` on modern Node, with each loading the proper build and no deep-import leaks. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: `"main"` to an ESM file and a `"files"` list, since `files` restricts which paths consumers can import
`"type":"module"` with `"main":"index.js"`, since Node transpiles ESM for CommonJS consumers on load
A `"module"` field to the ESM file and `"main"` to CJS, since Node picks the build by the importer
An `"exports"` map with conditions `"import"` for the ESM build and `"require"` for the CJS build

rubric: Conditional exports select the build and encapsulate internals.
The module field is a bundler convention; type alone does not provide dual builds; files only affects publishing.

items.prompt: Design a handler that calls two upstream services. Constraints: total deadline of 3 s, upstream work must stop if the deadline passes, and it must also stop if the client disconnects. Which design satisfies all?

options.label: Set `server.timeout = 3000` and rely on the socket closing to cancel upstream calls
Pass `AbortSignal.any([AbortSignal.timeout(3000), clientAbortSignal])` to each upstream `fetch`
Check `Date.now()` after each `await` and return early once 3 s have passed
Wrap the calls in `Promise.race` with a 3 s timer and leave the losing requests to finish

rubric: A combined abort signal cancels in-flight upstream work on timeout or disconnect.
Promise.race leaves work running; server.timeout does not cancel outgoing calls; polling cannot interrupt a pending await.

items.prompt: Design a retry policy for calling a flaky payment API from a Node worker. Constraints: avoid retry storms across many workers, never double-charge, and bound total retry time. Which design meets all?

options.label: Exponential backoff without jitter, generating a fresh request ID per attempt so each retry is tracked separately
Retry forever at a fixed 1 s interval, because a constant rate per worker cannot overload the API
Retry immediately up to 10 times, since fast retries minimise the window in which duplicate charges can occur
Exponential backoff with jitter and a max-elapsed cap, sending a stable idempotency key on each attempt

rubric: Jitter prevents synchronized retries, the capped duration bounds time, and the stable key makes retries safe.
Fresh IDs defeat idempotency; fixed intervals or immediate retries cause storms.

items.prompt: Design a `Transform` stream that converts raw network chunks into parsed objects from newline-delimited JSON. Constraints: handle JSON lines split across chunks, honour backpressure, and not lose a final line lacking a newline. Which design works?

options.label: Parse `chunk.toString()` as JSON in `transform`, with a `try/catch` that skips any chunk that fails to parse
Collect every chunk in an array, then split and parse all lines in `flush` and push the results at the end
Keep a leftover string, push parsed complete lines in `transform`, and parse the leftover in `flush`
Split each chunk on newline and parse every part, discarding the last part of each chunk as incomplete

rubric: Carrying remainder state and flushing it handles splits and a missing final newline.
Per-chunk parsing corrupts split lines; collecting everything defeats streaming and memory limits; discarding loses data.

items.prompt: A proposed upload endpoint uses `express.raw({limit:'2gb'})`, then `fs.writeFileSync(path, req.body)`. Requirements: 2 GB files, 256 MB memory budget, no leftover partial files when clients abort. Which elements are missing from this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Streaming `req` to disk with `stream.pipeline` instead of buffering the body
Deleting the partial file when the pipeline errors or the client aborts
Enforcing a byte limit while streaming and rejecting the request when exceeded
Switching `writeFileSync` to `writeFileSync` with the `flush` option, to prevent memory growth
Running more cluster workers, which gives each upload a larger memory budget

rubric: Streaming, a streaming size check and cleanup on failure meet memory and partial-file constraints.
More workers multiply memory use; flush options do not stop whole-body buffering.

items.prompt: You must add image resizing (about 150 ms CPU per image) to a Node API on an 8-core host. Constraints: event-loop latency stays low, memory stays bounded under a traffic spike, a crashing resize must not take down the API, and overload must fail fast. Which design meets all the constraints?

options.label: A pool of 6 workers fed by an unbounded in-memory queue, so no request is ever rejected during spikes
Run `sharp`-style resizing inline in handlers but call `setImmediate` between steps to keep the loop responsive
A fixed pool of about 6 workers with a bounded queue, replacing crashed workers and returning 503 when the queue is full
Start a new Worker per request and terminate it when done, so each crash is isolated from the API

rubric: A bounded pool caps CPU and memory, isolates crashes and sheds load.
Unbounded queues grow memory; per-request workers add startup and memory spikes; inline work still blocks the loop.
